difficultyReason: Scientific/methodological argument about a drug trial. The correct answer confirms a load-bearing assumption about the control group's comparability. Traps include a plausible-sounding irrelevant fact about dosage and a choice that strengthens a neighboring claim rather than the conclusion.
stimulus: Researchers conducting a clinical trial found that patients who received the experimental drug Veralox recovered from moderate influenza infections an average of two days faster than patients in the control group who received a placebo. The researchers concluded that Veralox itself caused the faster recovery.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Veralox was developed using a novel antiviral compound not found in any currently approved influenza medication.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Patients in the Veralox group and the placebo group had similar baseline health profiles and were infected with the same influenza strain.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The clinical trial was conducted at three different hospital sites to ensure geographic diversity among participants.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Several participants in the placebo group sought additional over-the-counter remedies during the trial period.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Veralox has also shown promising results in laboratory tests against other respiratory viruses.

explanations.correct: The argument's causal conclusion depends on the two groups being comparable — if patients in the Veralox group were healthier or had milder infections to begin with, the drug itself might not deserve credit. Choice B confirms that the groups were matched on baseline health and virus strain, closing the most obvious gap between the evidence and the causal conclusion.
explanations.A: Accurate but irrelevant. The novelty of the compound's chemistry tells us nothing about whether the trial design supports a causal conclusion. This is a topical but non-supporting fact.
explanations.B: Correct. Confirms the critical load-bearing assumption that the control and treatment groups were comparable, ruling out pre-existing group differences as an alternative explanation for the faster recovery.
explanations.C: Strengthens external validity (generalizability) but does not address whether Veralox caused faster recovery versus some confound within the trial — a different conclusion than the one drawn.
explanations.D: This is a disguised weakener. If placebo patients sought additional remedies, those remedies — not the absence of Veralox — may partly explain the difference, which actually introduces an alternative cause rather than ruling one out.
explanations.E: Strengthens a neighboring claim about Veralox's general antiviral properties, not the specific causal conclusion that Veralox caused faster influenza recovery in this trial.

difficultyReason: Environmental/policy argument with an implicit mechanism about carbon pricing reducing industrial emissions. The correct answer closes an analogy gap between past policy and the current proposal. Traps include an irrelevant comparison and a choice that introduces a rival cause.
stimulus: An environmental advocacy group argues that introducing a carbon tax on industrial emissions in the Lakewood region will significantly reduce those emissions within five years. They point to the fact that a neighboring region, Cedarvale, introduced a comparable carbon tax a decade ago and saw its industrial emissions drop by 30 percent over the following five years.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, provides the most support for the advocacy group's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Lakewood region's industrial sector is dominated by the same types of manufacturing industries as Cedarvale's was when its carbon tax was introduced.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Carbon taxes have been endorsed by a majority of environmental economists as an effective tool for reducing greenhouse gas emissions globally.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cedarvale's industrial emissions continued to decline for several years after the initial five-year period following the carbon tax's introduction.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Lakewood region recently enacted stricter environmental regulations that are independent of any proposed carbon tax.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Several Lakewood industries have already begun exploring renewable energy options in anticipation of future environmental legislation.

explanations.correct: The argument is analogical: because Cedarvale's carbon tax worked, Lakewood's will too. The analogy's weakest link is whether the two regions' industrial sectors are sufficiently similar. Choice A closes that gap by confirming that Lakewood's industries mirror the types that responded to the tax in Cedarvale, making the analogical inference much stronger.
explanations.A: Correct. Directly confirms the analogical premise by establishing industrial-sector similarity between Lakewood and Cedarvale, the critical gap the argument needs to bridge.
explanations.B: Unwarranted comparison. This is a broad global endorsement that does not specifically address whether Lakewood's situation resembles the contexts in which carbon taxes have worked. It strengthens a general claim, not the specific prediction.
explanations.C: Strengthens a different conclusion — that Cedarvale's long-term results were positive — rather than supporting the prediction that Lakewood will see emissions drop in the next five years.
explanations.D: Introduces an alternative cause. If Lakewood already has stricter independent regulations, those regulations — not the proposed carbon tax — might drive any future emission reductions, which undermines rather than supports attributing results to the carbon tax.
explanations.E: Accurate but irrelevant. Industry anticipation of future legislation tells us nothing decisive about whether the carbon tax specifically will cause the predicted five-year reduction.

difficultyReason: Historical/linguistic argument about a causal claim regarding written language standardization. The correct answer confirms the implicit mechanism linking trade network expansion to dialect convergence. Traps include an opposite-direction causal claim and an irrelevant historical fact.
stimulus: Historians of language have noted that the dialects spoken in the Aldenmere valley became significantly more uniform between the twelfth and fourteenth centuries. During this same period, long-distance trade networks connecting the valley's towns expanded considerably. The historians argue that the expansion of these trade networks caused the dialect convergence.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to support the historians' reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Written records from the thirteenth century show that Aldenmere merchants who traveled between towns began adopting vocabulary and pronunciations from each other's home dialects.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dialect convergence has also been observed in other valley regions of comparable geography during the medieval period.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Aldenmere valley's population grew substantially during the twelfth through fourteenth centuries due to improved agricultural yields.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Dialect convergence in the Aldenmere valley was already underway before the trade network expansion began in earnest.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The towns connected by the Aldenmere trade networks were located no more than two days' travel from one another.

explanations.correct: The historians' causal argument requires a mechanism: how would trade network expansion actually produce dialect convergence? Choice A supplies that mechanism directly — merchants traveling between towns adopted each other's linguistic features, constituting exactly the process by which trade contact would cause dialects to merge. This confirms the implicit causal link the argument depends on.
explanations.A: Correct. Supplies the missing causal mechanism — merchants engaged in cross-dialectal linguistic exchange — that bridges the premise (trade expansion) to the conclusion (dialect convergence), directly supporting the historians' causal claim.
explanations.B: Unwarranted comparison. Other valley regions experiencing dialect convergence could be explained by any number of shared geographic or demographic factors; without linking those cases to trade, this does not support the specific causal claim about Aldenmere.
explanations.C: Introduces an alternative cause. Population growth driven by agricultural yields is a rival explanation for dialect convergence (more mixing of people generally), which undermines the trade-network explanation rather than supporting it.
explanations.D: Opposite answer. If convergence was already underway before trade expansion, this directly weakens the causal claim by suggesting the trade networks were not the cause.
explanations.E: Accurate but irrelevant. The physical proximity of towns may be a background condition, but it does not explain why trade — rather than proximity alone — drove dialect convergence, nor does it confirm the causal mechanism the argument needs.
